prompt: Some people believe that the government should spend more money on public transportation, while others think it should focus on improving roads for private vehicles. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
essay:
The allocation of state expenditure on transport infrastructure remains a contentious policy issue. While proponents of private vehicle infrastructure argue that upgraded roads stimulate commerce and offer personal mobility, I believe that prioritizing public transit is a far more sustainable and equitable long-term strategy for urban development.

Advocates of expanding road networks point to economic efficiency and personal convenience. In many regional or suburban contexts, public transit networks cannot economically reach every household. For these communities, private automobiles remain essential for commuting and accessing vital services. Furthermore, commercial freight relies almost entirely on highways to distribute goods from industrial ports to regional distribution centers. When arterial highways suffer from severe bottlenecks, supply chains slow down, creating measurable economic drag. Expanding lane capacity and smoothing bypass routes can alleviate freight delays and accommodate workers whose schedules require flexible personal travel.

Conversely, investing heavily in public transportation yields decisive environmental and societal dividends. Modern urban centers face chronic air pollution and gridlock, neither of which road expansion resolves. Urban transport studies demonstrate the principle of "induced demand," where building wider highways simply attracts additional motorists, returning traffic to capacity within years. In contrast, high-capacity commuter rail, electric metro lines, and dedicated bus rapid transit (BRT) move thousands of passengers per hour using a fraction of the land area and energy per capita. A well-integrated mass transit system lowers urban carbon emissions, reduces reliance on imported fossil fuels, and democratizes mobility for lower-income demographics who cannot afford vehicle ownership, maintenance, and insurance.

In my view, prioritizing mass transit generates greater societal return on investment. Road expansion creates a vicious cycle of urban sprawl and automobile dependency, whereas efficient metro and bus systems drive compact, walkable economic development around transit hubs. While existing roads require baseline maintenance to ensure cargo flow and safety, the lion's share of infrastructure capital should target clean, reliable public transport networks to build resilient, accessible modern cities.
